title: Infix, Postfix and Prefix Conversion
quickIdea: Postfix writes the operator after its two operands, so no brackets are needed. Converting from infix needs one stack, holding operators and brackets, never operands.
remember: Precedence used by the standard conversion, highest first: brackets, then ^, then * and /, then + and -. ^ is right-associative; the others are left-associative unless a question says otherwise.

Shunting-yard rule: an operand goes straight to the output; an operator pops from the stack while the stack top has higher precedence, or equal precedence and the incoming operator is left-associative; a left bracket is pushed and a right bracket pops until its left bracket.

Prefix is produced by the same algorithm with the input read right to left, or by reversing the postfix string - reversing postfix gives prefix of the mirrored expression only when the operators are not reordered, so the safe method is the right-to-left pass.
A right-associative operator must NOT pop an equal-precedence operator from the stack. This one rule decides most exam questions.
Postfix of a + b * c - d ^ e ^ f is a b c * + d e f ^ ^ -.

example.prompt: GATE CSE 2004. With +, -, * left-associative and ^ right-associative, and precedence ^ > * > + > -, write the postfix form of a + b * c - d ^ e ^ f.
example.work: Highest precedence first: b * c becomes b c *. Right associativity groups d ^ e ^ f as d ^ (e ^ f), which becomes d e f ^ ^ - not d e ^ f ^. Now the expression is (a + (b * c)) - (d ^ (e ^ f)), whose postfix is a b c * + then d e f ^ ^ then the final minus: a b c * + d e f ^ ^ -.
example.answer: a b c * + d e f ^ ^ -, option (A) of the paper.

gateAngle: The examiner's lever is associativity, not precedence: every distractor differs by whether ^ grouped to the left or the right. Convert the highest-precedence subexpression first, then combine, and the operator stack never has to be simulated in full.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Write the postfix form of A + B * (C + D) / F + D * E.
variations.answer: A B C D + * F / + D E * +.
variations.why: Same method as the 2004 question with a bracket added: C + D becomes C D +, B * (C + D) becomes B C D + *, dividing by F gives B C D + * F /, and A plus that gives A B C D + * F / +. The trailing D * E is D E *, joined by the final +. The bracket, not associativity, is what changes here.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does infix-to-postfix conversion need only an operator stack and no operand stack?
variations.answer: Because operands are emitted in the order they are read; only operators and brackets have to be held back and reordered.
variations.why: This is GATE CSE 1997's question in substance. An operand's position in the output is already decided when it is read, so nothing about it needs remembering - the reordering work belongs entirely to the operators.

trap.what: Popping an equal-precedence operator when the incoming operator is right-associative.
trap.why: Right associativity means the incoming operator binds tighter to what follows it, so it must wait on the stack above the earlier one. Popping early turns a ^ (b ^ c) into (a ^ b) ^ c, a different expression.
trap.counterexample: With d = 2, e = 3, f = 2: d ^ (e ^ f) = 2^9 = 512, while (d ^ e) ^ f = 8^2 = 64. The postfix d e f ^ ^ and d e ^ f ^ evaluate to 512 and 64, so the two candidate answers are not merely different strings.

check.question: Write the postfix form of (a + b) * c.
check.explanation: The bracket forces a + b first, giving a b +, and the multiplication then applies to that result and c. Without the bracket, a + b * c would be a b c * +.
